Earth's Atmosphere.intro: The composition of Earth's atmosphere has changed dramatically over billions of years. Understanding this history is essential for C9.
Earth's Atmosphere.mnemonic: "Volcanoes Cooked Oxygen Nicely" — Volcanoes (early gases), Condensation (oceans formed), Oxygen (from photosynthesis), Nitrogen (accumulated as unreactive).

sections.title: The Early Atmosphere
sections.text: Billions of years ago, volcanic activity released gases that formed Earth's first atmosphere, rich in CO₂ and water vapour with almost no oxygen.
points: Volcanic outgassing — volcanoes released gases from inside Earth to form the early atmosphere
Main gases — carbon dioxide (CO₂), water vapour (H₂O), nitrogen (N₂); very little or no oxygen
Similar planets — early Earth's atmosphere resembled current atmospheres of Mars and Venus
No free oxygen — O₂ was absent; life as we know it could not have survived
High CO₂ — CO₂ concentrations far higher than today, making the early atmosphere very different

sections.title: How the Atmosphere Changed
sections.text: Over billions of years, cooling oceans, photosynthesis, and the accumulation of unreactive nitrogen gradually shifted the atmosphere to its current composition.
points: Ocean formation — water vapour condensed as Earth cooled, forming the oceans
CO₂ dissolved — CO₂ dissolved in the oceans and formed carbonate rocks, reducing atmospheric CO₂
Photosynthesis — early algae and plants evolved, removing CO₂ and releasing O₂ into the atmosphere
Oxygen rise — O₂ levels gradually increased over billions of years to ~21%
Nitrogen accumulation — N₂ built up because it is unreactive and not removed by any natural process
Ozone layer — O₃ formed from O₂ in the upper atmosphere, absorbing UV radiation and allowing life to colonise land

sections.title: Current Atmosphere
sections.text: Today's atmosphere has remained relatively stable for about 200 million years, though human activity is now altering its composition.
points: Nitrogen (N₂) — approximately 78% of the atmosphere; unreactive and stable
Oxygen (O₂) — approximately 21%; produced by photosynthesis and maintained by the carbon cycle
Argon (Ar) — approximately 0.9%; a noble gas and completely inert
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) — approximately 0.04%; essential for photosynthesis but rising due to human activity
Water vapour — variable (0–4%); plays a key role in the water cycle and greenhouse effect
Stability — the balance of photosynthesis and respiration has kept O₂ and CO₂ levels roughly constant for millions of years

callout.label: Current Composition
callout.text: 78% nitrogen (N₂), 21% oxygen (O₂), ~0.9% argon (Ar), ~0.04% carbon dioxide (CO₂), variable water vapour.

keyTerms.def: Release of gases from volcanoes that formed Earth's early atmosphere
Process by which plants/algae used CO₂ and produced O₂ — changed the atmosphere
Layer of O₃ in the stratosphere that absorbs UV radiation
Water vapour cooling and turning to liquid water — how the oceans first formed
The natural cycling of carbon between the atmosphere, organisms, oceans, and rocks
Rocks such as limestone formed when CO₂ dissolved in oceans and was deposited as sediment
An unreactive gas in Group 0 of the periodic table; argon is a noble gas in the atmosphere

examTips: The key process that increased O₂: photosynthesis by early algae and plants.
CO₂ decreased because of TWO processes — it dissolved in oceans AND was used in photosynthesis; give both in exam answers.
Nitrogen built up because it is unreactive — it was not produced by any single reaction, just not removed.
Learn the percentages: 78% N₂, 21% O₂, 0.9% Ar, 0.04% CO₂ — these numbers come up in multiple-choice questions.
commonMistakes: Saying nitrogen was produced by a specific process — it accumulated because it is unreactive and nothing removed it.
Forgetting that CO₂ also dissolved in the oceans, not just used in photosynthesis — always give both reasons.
Claiming the current atmosphere is exactly the same as billions of years ago — it has changed enormously over geological time.
clozePassages: The Earth's atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 1% argon, and 0.04% carbon dioxide, along with water vapour and trace gases. This composition has been relatively stable for the last 200 million years. Early in Earth's history, the atmosphere was very different — mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour, with almost no oxygen. The current atmosphere developed through volcanic activity, condensation of water, photosynthesis, and the evolution of life.

The early atmosphere of Earth was dominated by volcanic gases including carbon dioxide, water vapour, and nitrogen. As the Earth cooled, water vapour condensed to form the oceans. Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and was used by marine organisms, gradually reducing its atmospheric concentration. The evolution of photosynthetic organisms produced oxygen, which accumulated in the atmosphere over billions of years, eventually reaching its current level of about 21%.

The current proportions of gases in the atmosphere are maintained by a balance of processes. Photosynthesis removes CO₂ and produces O₂. Respiration and combustion consume O₂ and produce CO₂. The nitrogen cycle involves bacteria converting nitrogen between different forms. Human activities — particularly burning fossil fuels — are disrupting this balance by adding extra carbon dioxide to the atmosphere faster than natural processes can absorb it.

Greenhouse Effect.intro: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere, keeping Earth warm enough for life. Human activities are enhancing this effect, causing climate change.
Greenhouse Effect.mnemonic: "Cows Munch Warm Nights" — CO₂, Methane, Water vapour, Nitrous oxide — the four main greenhouse gases.

sections.title: How the Greenhouse Effect Works
sections.text: Greenhouse gases act like a blanket around Earth, trapping outgoing infrared radiation and warming the surface.
points: Short-wave solar radiation — UV and visible light pass through the atmosphere to Earth's surface
Absorption — Earth's surface absorbs solar radiation and warms up
Infrared re-emission — warmed Earth re-emits long-wave infrared radiation upwards
Greenhouse gas absorption — greenhouse gases absorb this infrared radiation
Re-emission in all directions — some infrared is re-emitted back towards Earth, trapping heat
Net warming — without this effect, Earth's average temperature would be −18°C instead of +15°C

sections.title: Greenhouse Gases
sections.text: Several gases contribute to the greenhouse effect; human activity has increased the concentration of many of them.
points: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) — from burning fossil fuels, deforestation, cement production
Methane (CH₄) — from livestock digestion, landfill, rice paddies, natural gas leaks; more potent than CO₂ per molecule
Water vapour (H₂O) — natural; increases as temperature rises (positive feedback)
Nitrous oxide (N₂O) — from fertilisers and agriculture
Human impact — industrial revolution has significantly raised CO₂ from ~280 ppm to over 420 ppm

sections.title: Climate Change Consequences
sections.text: The enhanced greenhouse effect is causing measurable changes to global climate with wide-ranging consequences.
points: Rising temperatures — global average surface temperatures have risen ~1°C since pre-industrial times
Melting ice — Arctic sea ice, Antarctic ice sheets, and glaciers are shrinking, raising sea levels
Extreme weather — more frequent and intense floods, droughts, heatwaves, and storms
Species distribution — changing habitats force species to move or face extinction
Agriculture — shifts in rainfall patterns and temperature disrupt food production globally
Ocean acidification — CO₂ dissolving in oceans lowers pH, threatening marine ecosystems

keyTerms.def: Natural process where greenhouse gases trap infrared radiation, warming Earth
Increased warming due to human-caused rise in greenhouse gas concentrations
Long-term changes in global climate patterns due to enhanced greenhouse effect
Long-wave electromagnetic radiation emitted by Earth's surface that greenhouse gases absorb
Total greenhouse gas emissions (in CO₂ equivalent) caused by an individual, event, or product
A measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps relative to CO₂ over 100 years
A cycle where rising temperature causes more warming, e.g. melting ice reduces reflectivity

examTips: The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life — the enhanced effect caused by humans is the problem; make this distinction clearly.
Methane is more potent than CO₂ as a greenhouse gas per molecule — useful to mention in 6-mark evaluation questions.
Be able to evaluate evidence for climate change — scientific consensus is overwhelming; ice core data shows CO₂ is at its highest in 800,000 years.
Know the difference between the greenhouse effect and the ozone hole — they are completely separate issues.
commonMistakes: Confusing the ozone hole (separate UV issue caused by CFCs) with the greenhouse effect (heat trapping by CO₂/CH₄).
Saying the greenhouse effect is entirely man-made — it is a natural process that is being enhanced by human activities.
Saying infrared radiation passes through greenhouse gases — it is absorbed and re-emitted, not transmitted.
clozePassages: The greenhouse effect is the trapping of heat energy by certain gases in the atmosphere. The main greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour, and nitrous oxide. These gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface and re-emit it in all directions, warming the planet. Without any greenhouse effect, Earth's average temperature would be about -18°C. The enhanced greenhouse effect from human activities is causing climate change.

Human activities are increasing the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide. Deforestation reduces the amount of CO₂ removed by photosynthesis. Agriculture, particularly livestock farming, produces methane through digestion and decomposition of manure. Rice paddies and landfill also produce methane. Nitrous oxide is released from fertilisers. These increases are causing the planet to warm.

The scientific evidence for human-caused climate change is overwhelming. Ice core data shows that atmospheric CO₂ levels are higher now than at any point in the past 800,000 years. Global average temperatures have risen by approximately 1°C since pre-industrial times. The consequences include rising sea levels, more extreme weather, changes in species distribution, and food and water shortages. International agreements such as the Paris Agreement aim to limit warming to 1.5°C.

Air Pollution.intro: Burning fossil fuels releases pollutant gases that damage health and the environment. Understanding sources, effects and solutions is required for C9.
Air Pollution.mnemonic: "Carbon Stays Naughty Passing Pollution" — CO, SO₂, NOₓ, Particulates, Prevention (catalytic converters) — the key pollutant sequence.

sections.title: Pollutants from Combustion
sections.text: Burning fossil fuels produces several harmful gases depending on whether combustion is complete or incomplete and whether impurities are present.
points: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) — greenhouse gas; from complete combustion of fossil fuels; contributes to climate change
Carbon monoxide (CO) — toxic, colourless, odourless; from incomplete combustion; binds to haemoglobin preventing O₂ transport
Soot/particulates — from incomplete combustion; cause respiratory problems and global dimming
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) — from sulfur impurities in fuels; dissolves in rainwater → sulfuric acid → acid rain
Nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) — N₂ + O₂ react at high engine temperatures; contribute to acid rain and photochemical smog
Unburned hydrocarbons — from incomplete combustion; contribute to smog and are toxic

sections.title: Effects of Pollutants
sections.text: Air pollutants have serious consequences for human health, ecosystems, and the built environment.
points: Acid rain — SO₂ and NOₓ dissolve in water; lowers pH of lakes (kills fish), erodes limestone buildings, damages trees
Carbon monoxide poisoning — CO binds to haemoglobin 200× more strongly than O₂; reduces oxygen in blood; can be fatal
Respiratory disease — particulates penetrate deep into lungs; worsen asthma, bronchitis, and cardiovascular disease
Global dimming — particulates reflect sunlight; reduce solar energy reaching Earth's surface
Photochemical smog — NOₓ reacts with sunlight and hydrocarbons; creates ground-level ozone; irritates eyes and lungs

sections.title: Solutions to Air Pollution
sections.text: Various technological and policy solutions can reduce harmful emissions from combustion.
points: Catalytic converters — convert CO and NOₓ to CO₂ and N₂ using a platinum catalyst; fitted in car exhausts
Flue gas desulfurisation — removes SO₂ from power station emissions by reacting with calcium oxide or limestone
Low-sulfur fuels — reducing sulfur content in petrol and diesel cuts SO₂ emissions
Renewable energy — replacing fossil fuels with wind, solar, and hydroelectric power eliminates combustion pollutants
Legislation — emission standards and clean air laws limit how much pollution industries and vehicles can produce

keyTerms.def: Toxic gas from incomplete combustion — binds to haemoglobin
Acidic gas from burning sulfur-containing fuels — causes acid rain
Rain with lower than normal pH caused by SO₂ and NOₓ dissolving in water
Device in car exhaust that converts CO and NOₓ to CO₂ and N₂
Tiny solid particles (soot) from incomplete combustion — cause respiratory damage
Gases formed when N₂ and O₂ react at high temperatures in engines — contribute to acid rain and smog
Industrial process that removes SO₂ from power station exhaust gases using calcium oxide

examTips: CO is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin — prevents oxygen transport. State this mechanism clearly in exam answers.
SO₂ + H₂O → sulfurous/sulfuric acid → acid rain. Know the chain of reactions.
Catalytic converters reduce CO and NOₓ — they do NOT reduce CO₂; they actually produce it from CO.
Know two solutions for each pollutant — e.g. for SO₂: low-sulfur fuels AND flue gas desulfurisation.
commonMistakes: Saying catalytic converters reduce CO₂ — they convert CO to CO₂, so actually produce more CO₂ while reducing toxic emissions.
Confusing CO (toxic, colourless, odourless) with CO₂ (not directly toxic at normal concentrations).
Forgetting that NOₓ formation requires high temperature — it is the temperature in the engine that causes N₂ and O₂ to react.
clozePassages: Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas produced by incomplete combustion of fuels in car engines and gas appliances. It is colourless and odourless, making it difficult to detect. It binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells more strongly than oxygen, preventing oxygen transport and causing suffocation. Catalytic converters in car exhausts convert carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide by oxidation over a platinum catalyst.

Sulfur dioxide is produced when fuels containing sulfur impurities are burned. It dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain, which damages buildings, kills trees, and acidifies lakes and rivers. Nitrogen oxides form in hot car engines when nitrogen and oxygen in the air react at high temperatures. They also contribute to acid rain and the formation of photochemical smog. Low-sulfur fuels and catalytic converters help reduce these pollutants.

Particulate matter from combustion and industrial processes contributes to air pollution. Fine particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and cause respiratory and cardiovascular problems. Carbon particles (soot) produced by incomplete combustion absorb heat and contribute to climate change when they settle on ice and snow. Reducing air pollution requires cleaner fuels, better emission controls, and a shift away from fossil fuels towards renewable energy sources.
